passage:
Tuesday. The list came out and Noor's name wasn't on it. Thomas's was. Noor sat in the parking lot with her hands on the steering wheel, relieved and sick about being relieved. She texted Thomas, "I'm so sorry." He replied with a thumbs-up and nothing else.

Thursday. Noor stopped saying sorry. She opened her contacts and sent Thomas the names of two hiring managers she knew, plus a note: "Tell them I recommended you." She also asked whether he'd like a written recommendation for his portfolio.

The following Wednesday. Thomas wrote back, "Thank you for not disappearing." They had coffee. Thomas talked about the layoff for a while, and Noor mostly listened. A month later, one of the managers invited him to interview. Noor didn't say anything grand. She just kept the coffee going.

qa.q: How did Thomas first reply to Noor's apology?
qa.a: Thomas replied with a thumbs-up and nothing else.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling in the parking lot?
qa.a: Noor felt relieved to keep her job and sick about being relieved, which shows guilt about surviving when Thomas was laid off.

qa.q: What did Noor do that turned her guilt into help?
qa.a: She shared two hiring managers' names, offered to be a reference and to write a recommendation, and later kept meeting Thomas for coffee.

qa.q: What did Thomas's thank-you suggest about how he had seen Noor's earlier silence?
qa.a: Thomas's thanks for not disappearing suggests he might have feared that laid-off people get avoided, so Noor's steady presence mattered to him.

grounding: A survivor of layoffs feels guilty and turns it into contacts, recommendations and steady presence for a laid-off friend.

passage: Naveen, you keep saying you feel terrible that you still have a job and Arun doesn't. I understand. When I was twenty-four, I was a young woman at a textile export house in Tiruppur, and they let go of half the design team. I stayed. My friend Leela went. The next week I couldn't look at her empty desk. When she called, I let it ring. I told myself I didn't know what to say. That was the worst thing I did, avoiding her because I felt guilty. After a month, my mother said, "Your guilt doesn't feed her family. Do something." So I did. I sent Leela's portfolio to four firms I knew, wrote a recommendation letter, and took her for lunch. She got a job in Coimbatore. We still laugh about that month. So don't avoid Arun. Pick up the phone. That's what Uma-paati learned.

qa.q: How many firms did Uma send Leela's portfolio to?
What did Uma feel when she saw Leela's empty desk?
qa.a: She felt guilty and uncomfortable for keeping her job, so she avoided Leela and let her calls ring.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed what Uma did?
qa.a: After her mother's words, Uma sent Leela's portfolio to firms, wrote a recommendation and took her to lunch.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt when Uma stopped answering her calls?
qa.a: Leela probably felt hurt and alone, perhaps wondering whether their friendship had ended along with her job.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling guilty for surviving a layoff, first avoiding a friend, then helping with referrals and a recommendation.

passage:
The layoff list had come out on Monday, and by Wednesday Gautam's floor at the Gurugram office was half empty. Vikas, his desk-mate for three years, was on the list. Gautam wasn't.
He felt guilty every time he walked past Vikas's cleared desk. He had written a long sad post online about "losing family at work", and it got two hundred likes. Vikas had not liked it.
That night, with the building's lift broken and his phone at ten per cent, Gautam climbed nine floors and sat on the stairs with his laptop. He opened a message to Vikas instead of another post. "I'm sorry. I don't know what to say, but I know what I can do." He wrote a recommendation on Vikas's work profile, emailed two managers he knew at other firms with Vikas's resume, and deleted the post.
Vikas replied at midnight: "Thanks, bro. That actually helps."

qa.q: How many likes did Gautam's post get?
What was Gautam feeling as he walked past Vikas's cleared desk?
qa.a: He felt guilty and uncomfortable for keeping the job while Vikas, a desk-mate of three years, lost one.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what did Gautam do instead?
qa.a: His sad post performed grief without helping; instead he wrote Vikas a recommendation, sent Vikas's resume to two managers, and deleted the post.

qa.q: How might Vikas have seen Gautam's post compared with his message?
qa.a: Vikas likely found the post empty or even hurtful, but felt genuinely helped and grateful for the direct message and referrals.

grounding: The protagonist feels guilty for keeping his job; he moves from performing grief online to referrals and a recommendation for his friend.
